flashcard_questions.q: What is a hot desert biome?
flashcard_questions.a: A biome that receives less than 250 mm of precipitation per year.

flashcard_questions.q: Between which latitudes are hot deserts typically found?
flashcard_questions.a: Between 20° and 30° north and south of the equator.

flashcard_questions.q: Which continent has no hot desert?
Why do hot deserts receive so little rainfall?
flashcard_questions.a: Air sinks at around 30° latitude and warms as it descends, so few clouds form.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the diurnal temperature range?
flashcard_questions.a: The difference between daytime and night-time temperatures.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do hot deserts have such a large diurnal temperature range?
flashcard_questions.a: The lack of cloud cover lets heat escape rapidly after sunset.

flashcard_questions.q: How hot can daytime temperatures in a hot desert become?
How cold can hot desert temperatures fall at night?
What proportion of hot desert landscape is made up of sand dunes?
Why does desert soil contain very little humus?
flashcard_questions.a: Rainfall is too low for the bacteria that decompose dead material.

flashcard_questions.q: How do the spines of a cactus reduce water loss?
flashcard_questions.a: Their tiny surface area cuts evaporation compared with broad leaves.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does a cactus have thick waxy skin?
flashcard_questions.a: It forms a waterproof coating that reduces water loss through evaporation.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the quiver tree do to its own branches in severe drought?
flashcard_questions.a: It cuts them off and seals the wound to reduce water loss.

flashcard_questions.q: What do the humps of a camel actually store?
flashcard_questions.a: Fat, which can be broken down into energy and water.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the fennec fox have large bat-like ears?
flashcard_questions.a: The ears radiate body heat and help the fox stay cool.

notes: 15 cards: 2 term-to-definition (hot desert, diurnal range), 4 case-fact cards with one figure each (latitude band, 45°C, 10°C, 25% dunes), 1 distribution card (no desert in Europe), 3 process-to-effect on climate and soil (sinking air, cloud cover, humus), 5 adaptation cause-to-consequence cards naming the species (cactus spines, cactus skin, quiver tree, camel humps, fennec ears). Quiver tree white powder, fennec nocturnal behaviour and camel foot shape were trimmed to stay within 15. The camel hump card deliberately corrects the fat-not-water misconception the lesson flags.
